w: Africa's first mosque started as a general's tent - Amr ibn al-As camped here in 642 CE founding Fustat, Egypt's first Islamic capital, then raised a mosque on the spot. Rebuilding since means nothing original survives, but for 600 years this was the region's top centre of Islamic learning, until Al-Azhar took over.
s: Africa's first mosque, born from a general's tent
_facts: Mosque in the Fustat neighbourhood of Old Cairo, built c. 642 CE as the centre of the newly founded capital Fustat
The first mosque built in Egypt and one of the first in Africa
For 600 years an important centre of Islamic learning, until replaced by Al-Azhar Mosque
Location was the site of Amr ibn al-As's former tent; due to extensive reconstruction nothing of the original building remains
An active mosque, open to visitors and tourists when prayers are not taking place

w: Seat of the Coptic Orthodox Pope since it was consecrated in 1968, this Abbassia cathedral held the title of largest church in Africa and the Middle East until a new one overtook it in 2019. It is dedicated to Saint Mark the Evangelist, founder of the Coptic Church in Egypt, and holds relics tied to his life inside.
s: Africa's biggest cathedral, for over 50 years
_facts: Coptic church in the Abbassia District, seat of the Coptic Orthodox Pope
Built under Pope Cyril VI of Alexandria, consecrated 25 June 1968
Dedicated to Saint Mark the Evangelist, an apostle and founder of the Coptic Orthodox Church; relics of his life are kept inside
Was the largest cathedral in Africa and the Middle East until the new Nativity Cathedral opened in 2019

w: Millions of volumes fill Dar el-Kotob's seven-story building on the Nile Corniche, including some of the oldest Arabic-language manuscripts anywhere. It is Egypt's largest library, with a national archive in an annex next door - a record of the country's social and political history, though closed to the public.
s: Millions of volumes, some the world's oldest
_facts: Largest library in Egypt, non-profit government organization, houses several million volumes
Contains a vast variety of Arabic-language and other Eastern manuscripts, said to be the oldest in the world
Main library is a seven-story building in Ramlet Boulaq, a district of Cairo, on the Nile Corniche
National Archives housed in an annex, significant for Egyptian social and political history, not open to the public

w: Twenty-two royal mummies - eighteen kings, four queens - crossed Cairo in a 2021 procession dubbed the Pharaohs' Golden Parade to reach this museum's official inauguration. The 50,000 artifacts inside trace Egyptian civilization from prehistory to the modern era, giving the mummies a permanent home in Old Cairo.
s: Where the Pharaohs' Golden Parade came to rest
_facts: Museum in Old Cairo, partially opened 2017, officially inaugurated 3 April 2021
Inauguration involved moving 22 mummies (18 kings, 4 queens) from the Egyptian Museum in an event called the Pharaohs' Golden Parade
Displays a collection of 50,000 artifacts, presenting Egyptian civilization from prehistoric times to the modern era

w: The Khedive built Africa's first opera house for the Suez Canal's opening in 1869; two years later, Verdi's Aida had its world premiere there. Built almost entirely of wood, it burned down in 1971 - only two statues survived. Cairo went without one for nearly twenty years; the site is now a parking garage.
s: Aida's birthplace is now a parking garage
_facts: Oldest opera house in Africa and the Middle East, inaugurated 1 November 1869, burned down 28 October 1971
Built on the orders of Khedive Ismail to celebrate the opening of the Suez Canal; made mostly of wood, seated about 850
Verdi's Rigoletto was the first opera performed there in 1869; Aida's world premiere took place there on 24 December 1871 after delays from the Franco-Prussian War
The all-wooden building was consumed by fire in 1971; only two statues by Mohamed Hassan survived
Cairo was without an opera house for nearly two decades until 1988; the site was later rebuilt into a multi-story concrete car garage

w: Egypt's second-oldest scientific institute, established in 1798, specializes in Egyptology and remains a working research center for the discipline today - one of the oldest learned societies anywhere still doing the job it was built for.
s: Egypt's oldest home for the study of Egypt
_facts: Scientific institute and research center in Cairo, specializes in Egyptology
Established in 1798, the second oldest scientific institute in Egypt after Al-Azhar University

w: Four bronze lions by French sculptor Henri Alfred Jacquemart, cast in the late 19th century, still guard this Nile crossing - older than the swing-bridge itself, a 1931 rebuild of the first bridge ever to span the Nile in central Cairo. Officially the Khedive Ismail Bridge, everyone just calls it Qasr al-Nil.
s: Four bronze lions guarding the Nile crossing
_facts: Historic swing bridge dating from 1931, originally named Khedive Ismail Bridge, replaced the first bridge to span the Nile in central Cairo
Connects Tahrir Square in Downtown Cairo to the southern end of Gezira/Zamalek Island
Four large bronze lion statues stand at its east and west approaches, late 19th-century works by French sculptor Henri Alfred Jacquemart

w: Named for the Fatimid caliph who founded Cairo in the 10th century, this was the city's main artery for a thousand years - the Qasaba, lined with souks, mosques and charitable foundations rulers built to outdo one another. The Bayn al-Qasrayn stretch alone packs in some of Islamic Cairo's densest architecture.
s: Cairo's original main street, a thousand years old
_facts: Major north-south street in the walled city of historic Cairo, dating to the city's 10th-century Fatimid founding, named for caliph Al-Mu'izz
Historically the most important artery of the city, referred to as the Qasaba; main axis of the city's souks and economic zones
Attracted the construction of many monumental religious and charitable buildings by Egypt's rulers and elites
The Bayn al-Qasrayn area along the street is a dense repository of historic Islamic architecture

w: One of only three gates left standing in old Cairo's city wall, Bab al-Futuh - the 'Conquest Gate' - has guarded the northern end of al-Mu'izz Street since the Fatimid period, rebuilt in its current form in the late 11th century. Its sister gates, Bab al-Nasr and Bab Zuwayla, still stand nearby.
s: One of Cairo's last three medieval city gates
_facts: One of three remaining gates in the city wall of old Cairo, located at the northern end of al-Mu'izz Street
The other two remaining gates are Bab al-Nasr and Bab Zuwayla
Built during the Fatimid period, originally in the 10th century, rebuilt in its current form in the late 11th century

w: At 130 metres, Al-Fath's minaret is the third tallest in the world and the tallest thing over Ramses Square - a 1990 addition and one of Cairo's largest mosques. In August 2013 it became a flashpoint during Egypt's post-coup unrest, when clashes here left protesters dead or injured and the mosque was shut for a time.
s: The world's third-tallest minaret, over Ramses Square
_facts: Mosque in Ramses Square, Downtown Cairo, completed 1990, one of the largest mosques in the city
Its 130-metre-tall minaret is the tallest in Cairo and the third tallest minaret in the world
Site of the Second Ramses Incident on 16 August 2013 during post-coup unrest, resulting in deaths and injuries of protesters and the mosque's subsequent shutdown
